questions.prompt: A scalar function \(V\) certifies that an equilibrium at the origin is asymptotically stable when
options: \(V\) is positive definite and \(\dot{V}\) along the dynamics is negative definite
\(V\) is positive at even one point near the origin
\(\dot{V}\) is positive definite, so trajectories climb the bowl
\(V\) equals the output \(y\)
questions.explanation: The bowl has to be positive everywhere except at the origin, and motion has to decrease it. One positive sample does not make \(V\) positive definite. A positive derivative drives trajectories away. The output is not a Lyapunov function unless it happens to meet both tests, which a general \(y\) does not.

questions.explanation: \(2 a P = -q\) with \(a = -3\) and \(q = 12\) gives \(-6P = -12\), so \(P = 2\). The positive root of the state weight, 12, is \(q\), not \(P\). Flipping the sign of \(a\) would make \(P\) negative, and a negative \(P\) is not a certificate.

questions.explanation: \(\dot{V} = 2x \dot{x} = 2x(-4x) = -8x^2\). At \(x = 0.5\), that is \(-8 \cdot 0.25 = -2\). Dropping the 2 from the chain rule leaves \(-4x^2 = -1\). Using \(+4x\) as the vector field flips the sign and gives \(+2\).

questions.prompt: For \(\dot{x} = a x\) with \(a < 0\), you pick \(q > 0\) and solve \(2 a P = -q\). Write \(P\) in the names a and q.
questions.explanation: Solving \(2 a P = -q\) gives \(P = -q/(2a)\). Because \(a\) is negative, this \(P\) is positive. The reciprocal \( -2a/q \) inverts the certificate. Dropping the 2 leaves a value twice too large.

questions.prompt: For \(A = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & 1 \\ -2 & -3 \end{bmatrix}\) and \(Q = I\), the solution of \(A^T P + PA = -Q\) has upper-left entry
questions.explanation: Write \(P = \begin{bmatrix} p & q \\ q & r \end{bmatrix}\). The equation forces \(q = 1/4\), \(r = 1/4\), and \(p - 3q - 2r = 0\), so \(p = 5/4 = 1.25\). The off-diagonal entry \(1/4\) is not the upper-left entry. The trace of \(A\), which is \(-3\), is not an entry of \(P\).
questions.figure: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 200 130" role="img" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.6" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-linejoin="round" font-family="sans-serif" font-size="12"><title>a 2 by 2 state matrix</title><text x="28" y="78" text-anchor="middle" font-size="28" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">[</text><text x="168" y="78" text-anchor="middle" font-size="28" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">]</text><text x="98" y="58" text-anchor="middle" font-size="16" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">0   1</text><text x="98" y="86" text-anchor="middle" font-size="16" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">-2   -3</text></svg>
questions.figure_alt: A 2 by 2 matrix with first row 0, 1 and second row -2, -3.

questions.prompt: Put these steps in the order you would use to test a linear system with the Lyapunov equation.
questions.explanation: You pick \(Q\) first, because the equation is linear in \(P\) once \(Q\) is known. Solving comes next. Positive definiteness of \(P\) is the test, not an assumption you skip. Only then does the quadratic \(x^T P x\) certify asymptotic stability. Checking \(P\) before solving has nothing to check.
questions.figure: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 280 210" role="img" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.6" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-linejoin="round" font-family="sans-serif" font-size="12"><title>a quadratic level curve around the origin</title><line x1="28" y1="104" x2="256" y2="104"/><polygon points="256,104 249.6,106.7 249.6,101.3" fill="currentColor" stroke="none"/><line x1="140" y1="186" x2="140" y2="24"/><polygon points="140,24 142.7,30.4 137.3,30.4" fill="currentColor" stroke="none"/><text x="250" y="120" text-anchor="end" font-size="11" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">x1</text><text x="148" y="20" text-anchor="start" font-size="11" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">x2</text><ellipse cx="140" cy="104" rx="86" ry="46"/><line x1="54" y1="104" x2="226" y2="104" stroke-dasharray="4 3"/><line x1="140" y1="58" x2="140" y2="150" stroke-dasharray="4 3"/></svg>
questions.figure_alt: An ellipse centered on the origin, longer along one axis.
steps: Choose a symmetric positive definite matrix Q.
Solve A transpose P + P A = -Q for the symmetric unknown P.
Test whether that P is positive definite.
If it is, conclude that the origin of x-dot = A x is asymptotically stable.

questions.prompt: A note applies \(V(x) = x^2\) to \(\dot{x} = x\). One step is wrong.
questions.explanation: \(\dot{V} = 2x \cdot x = 2x^2\) is positive, so trajectories climb the bowl. Calling it negative definite reverses the test. \(V\) itself is a fine bowl, the general rule in the next step is right, and the same bowl does certify the stable scalar system \(\dot{x} = -x\).
questions.figure: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 280 210" role="img" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.6" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-linejoin="round" font-family="sans-serif" font-size="12"><title>a quadratic level curve around the origin</title><line x1="28" y1="104" x2="256" y2="104"/><polygon points="256,104 249.6,106.7 249.6,101.3" fill="currentColor" stroke="none"/><line x1="140" y1="186" x2="140" y2="24"/><polygon points="140,24 142.7,30.4 137.3,30.4" fill="currentColor" stroke="none"/><text x="250" y="120" text-anchor="end" font-size="11" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">x1</text><text x="148" y="20" text-anchor="start" font-size="11" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">x2</text><ellipse cx="140" cy="104" rx="86" ry="46"/><line x1="54" y1="104" x2="226" y2="104" stroke-dasharray="4 3"/><line x1="140" y1="58" x2="140" y2="150" stroke-dasharray="4 3"/></svg>
questions.figure_alt: An ellipse centered on the origin, longer along one axis.
steps: \(V(x) = x^2\) is positive for every \(x \ne 0\), and \(V(0) = 0\).
Along \(\dot{x} = x\), the derivative is \(\dot{V} = 2x^2\), and that derivative is negative definite.
A certificate needs a positive definite \(V\) and a negative definite derivative together.
reasons: The derivative 2x^2 is positive, so it is not a certificate for this vector field.
V(x) = x^2 is negative at the origin, so the first step already failed.
A positive derivative is exactly what asymptotic stability requires.

questions.prompt: Along a trajectory, \(\dot{V} = 0\) while \(V\) is positive definite. This \(V\)
options: proves exponential stability on its own
does not prove asymptotic stability, because the bowl is not strictly decreasing
proves that the origin is unstable
says that \(V\) fails to be positive definite
questions.explanation: Asymptotic stability needs the derivative to be negative definite, not merely non-positive. A zero derivative can belong to a conserved oscillation. It does not prove instability either, and it says nothing against the positive definiteness of \(V\).

questions.prompt: Which of these are Lyapunov certificates for asymptotic stability of the system written with them?
options: \(V = x^2\) along \(\dot{x} = -2x\)
\(V = -x^2\) along \(\dot{x} = -2x\)
\(V = x^2\) along \(\dot{x} = 2x\)
\(V = 3x^2\) along \(\dot{x} = -2x\)
questions.explanation: For \(\dot{x} = -2x\), both \(V = x^2\) and \(V = 3x^2\) are positive definite and their derivatives \(-4x^2\) and \(-12x^2\) are negative definite. \(V = -x^2\) is negative, so it is not a bowl. Along \(\dot{x} = 2x\), the derivative of \(x^2\) is positive, so that pair certifies nothing.

questions.explanation: \(\dot{V} = 8x \dot{x} = 8x(-0.5 x) = -4x^2\). At \(x = 1.5\), \(-4 \cdot 2.25 = -9\). Using \(V\) itself as the derivative gives \(4 \cdot 2.25 = 9\), the wrong sign and the wrong object. Halving because the vector field has a 0.5 leaves \(-2\), which drops the chain-rule factor.

questions.prompt: The matrix \(P\) in \(A^T P + PA = -Q\) is
options: the plant gain
an orthogonal matrix you may choose freely
the input matrix of the state equation
the unknown you solve for, and it certifies stability only when it is positive definite
questions.explanation: \(Q\) is the matrix you choose, positive definite. \(P\) is what the linear equation returns. A positive definite \(P\) makes \(x^T P x\) a Lyapunov function. \(P\) is not the plant, not an arbitrary rotation, and not \(B\).
questions.figure: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 200 130" role="img" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.6" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-linejoin="round" font-family="sans-serif" font-size="12"><title>a symmetric unknown matrix</title><text x="28" y="78" text-anchor="middle" font-size="28" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">[</text><text x="168" y="78" text-anchor="middle" font-size="28" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">]</text><text x="98" y="58" text-anchor="middle" font-size="16" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">p   q</text><text x="98" y="86" text-anchor="middle" font-size="16" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">q   r</text></svg>

questions.prompt: The Lyapunov equation has a unique solution, but that solution is not positive definite. For \(\dot{x} = Ax\) this means
options: the origin is asymptotically stable anyway, because a solution exists
\(Q\) was illegal, so the test is void
the origin is not asymptotically stable
every eigenvalue of \(A\) is zero
questions.explanation: For a linear system the equation produces a positive definite \(P\), for every positive definite \(Q\), exactly when every eigenvalue of \(A\) has a negative real part. A solution that fails to be positive definite means the origin is not asymptotically stable. Existence of some symmetric \(P\) is weaker. The failure does not require every eigenvalue to be zero, and a legal \(Q\) is what made the test meaningful.
